narrative:
The model estimates an 85% chance that you will leave your current job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This high probability reflects patterns the system sees in your overall profile compared to others who tend to stay.

The three factors that most strongly influenced this outlook, in order of importance, were your total years of professional experience, the length of time you have spent in your current role, and whether you have received other job offers while working here. 

Your 6–10 years of overall experience pushed the prediction toward leaving. While many employees predicted to stay have shorter careers (1–5 years is most common among stayers), the model sees mid-level experience as a point where people often begin exploring new opportunities. Similarly, having spent only 1–5 years in your present organization also contributed to the “will leave” direction; this is actually the most frequent range among those expected to stay, yet in combination with your broader career stage it signals readiness for change. Finally, the fact that you have received other job opportunities during your time here was a notable push toward leaving. Most employees the model expects to stay do not report receiving such offers.

Taken together, these elements suggest you are at a natural career transition point where external options become attractive. The organization should discuss retention strategies with you, such as clearer promotion paths or enhanced development support, while you may wish to openly explore whether your current role still aligns with your longer-term goals.
